Jean-Jacques Rousseau considered the Discourses and the Florentine Histories more representative of Machiavelli's true philosophy than The Prince. In The Social Contract he wrote that the contradiction between The Prince and the Discourses showed that this thinker had been studied only by superficial or corrupt readers. The Discourses were written around 1517 and published after his death, with papal privilege, in 1531.
dissolution-of-czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was created with the end of Austria-Hungary after the First World War. In 1918, at a meeting in Pittsburgh, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and other Czech and Slovak representatives signed the Pittsburgh Agreement, which promised a common state of two equal nations, Slovaks and Czechs. The Czechoslovak Constitution of 1920, however, specified a single Czechoslovak nation. Political tension followed between Czechoslovakists and those seeking greater autonomy for the Slovaks. In March 1939, under pressure from Adolf Hitler, the First Slovak Republic was created as a German satellite state, and after the war the two parts were reunited in the Third Czechoslovak Republic. In 1969 the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic became constituent states of the federation.

After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule, many Czechs and Slovaks wanted to keep a federal state. By 1991 the Czech Republic's GDP per capita was some 20 per cent higher than Slovakia's, and transfer payments from the Czech budget to Slovakia stopped in January 1991. Czech parties had little presence in Slovakia and the reverse. The government demanded continued control from Prague, while Slovaks asked for decentralisation, and leading Slovak parties, notably the Slovak National Party, advocated looser complete independence and sovereignty.

Historians debate whether the dissolution was inevitable, pointing to differences between the two nations dating from Austria-Hungary and to the 1968 constitution with its minority veto, or the result of events between 1989 and 1992. The partition took effect at the end of 1992, and, unlike the breakup of Yugoslavia, it brought no violence. No referendum was held, and the decision was unpopular at the time.

The national territory was divided along the existing internal borders, with disputes over a few places settled by negotiation, compensation and a treaty. Most federal assets, including army equipment and rail and air infrastructure, were divided in a ratio of two to one, the approximate ratio of the Czech and Slovak populations. The two states first kept the Czechoslovak koruna, but adopted separate currencies in February 1993. Each republic kept its own symbols, the Czech lion and the Slovak double cross. Neither state claimed to be the sole successor, Czechoslovakia's membership in the United Nations ended, and both were admitted as new states on 19 January 1993.

A customs union remained until both countries joined the European Union on 1 May 2004. On the dissolution all Czechoslovak citizens became citizens of the Czech Republic or Slovakia according to criteria such as residence and birthplace. Soon afterwards polls showed many people on both sides had opposed the split.
dissolution-of-the-soviet-union: Mikhail Gorbachev was elected General Secretary on 11 March 1985, just over four hours after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He meant to revive a stagnating economy and came to see that this required reforming political and social structures. His glasnost allowed nationalist movements and ethnic disputes to be expressed and to grow into dominant political forces. Commentators also point to chronic economic stagnation and the burden of the arms race with the United States.

In 1989 limited competitive elections were held for a new Congress of People's Deputies, and the revolutions of 1989 in the Warsaw Pact countries increased pressure for republican autonomy. Estonia was the first republic to declare state sovereignty, on 16 November 1988, and Lithuania the first to declare independence, in March 1990. In 1990 all fifteen republics held competitive elections, and the Communist Party lost them in five.

On 17 March 1991 a Union-wide referendum was held in which 77.85 per cent of voters endorsed keeping a reformed Soviet Union; the Baltic republics, Armenia, Georgia and Moldova boycotted it. In August 1991 communist hardliners tried to overthrow Gorbachev. The coup failed, but the turmoil weakened the central government, and many republics declared independence in the following days and months.

On 8 December the leaders of the Russian, Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics signed the Belovezha Accords, declared that the Soviet Union no longer existed and set up the Commonwealth of Independent States. Kazakhstan was the last republic to declare independence, on 16 December. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and passed his powers, including control of the nuclear launch codes, to Boris Yeltsin, and the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin. On 26 December the Soviet of the Republics formally dissolved the Soviet Union.

The dissolution marked the culmination of the revolutions of 1989 and the end of the Cold War. Russia became the recognised successor state and continued the Soviet seat at the United Nations. Several successor states kept close links with Russia through the Commonwealth, while the Baltic states moved towards the West. The end of Soviet aid brought crisis to Cuba and North Korea, and disputes over territory and minorities led to conflicts in some successor states.
divine-comedy: Dante Alighieri belonged to the Guelphs, who in general favoured the papacy over the Holy Roman Emperor. Florence's Guelphs split around 1300 into the White Guelphs and the Black Guelphs, and the White Guelphs later supported greater imperial power in Italy. Dante was among the White Guelphs exiled in 1302 after troops under Charles of Valois entered the city at the request of Pope Boniface VIII, who supported the Black Guelphs. The exile lasted the rest of his life and shows throughout the poem, from prophecies of his banishment to the damnation of some of his opponents.

The work was originally titled Comedìa. Dante used the word because poems in the ancient world were classed as high (tragedy) or low (comedy), and low poems had happy endings and everyday language. The adjective Divina first appears in Giovanni Boccaccio's Trattatello in laude di Dante, written between 1351 and 1355.

The poem has 14,233 lines in three cantiche, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, each of 33 cantos, and an introductory canto brings the total to 100. Its verse form is terza rima, in tercets of eleven-syllable lines. The story is told in the first person and runs from the night before Good Friday to the Wednesday after Easter in the spring of 1300. Virgil guides Dante through Hell and most of Purgatory, Beatrice from the end of Purgatorio, and Bernard of Clairvaux through the last cantos.

Hell has nine circles, Mount Purgatory nine rings crowned by the Garden of Eden, and Heaven nine celestial spheres beneath the Empyrean. Each punishment in Hell is a contrapasso, a symbolic instance of poetic justice: in Canto XX the fortune-tellers must walk with their heads turned backwards. Allegorically the poem represents the soul's journey towards God.

According to the Italian Dante Society, no manuscript in Dante's own hand survives, although some 800 copies from the 14th and 15th centuries are listed. Giovanni da Serravalle made the first complete translation, into Latin prose, in 1416, and Enrique de Villena completed a Castilian prose version in 1428. The first printed edition appeared at Foligno on 11 April 1472, in 300 copies, of which fourteen survive.

The poem was recognised as a masterpiece in the centuries after it was written, largely fell into obscurity during the Enlightenment, and was rediscovered in the English-speaking world by William Blake and the Romantic writers of the 19th century. Erich Auerbach held that it inaugurated literary realism in modern fiction. In 1919 Miguel Asín Palacios argued that Dante drew on the Islamic tradition of Muhammad's night journey to heaven, but Francesco Gabrieli and other scholars have not found the claim convincing.
division-of-korea: Korea had been a nominal protectorate of Japan after the Russo-Japanese War ended in 1905 and was formally annexed in 1910, when Emperor Gojong was deposed. Nationalist and radical groups struggled for independence but never united in one movement, and the Korean Provisional Government in exile in the Republic of China gained wide recognition only with the Second World War.

At the Cairo Conference in November 1943 Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek declared that Korea would in due course become free and independent. Roosevelt raised a trusteeship with Joseph Stalin at Tehran and Yalta, and Stalin did not object but wanted it short. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945 and advanced quickly into the north, which made the United States anxious that it would occupy the whole peninsula.

On 10 August 1945 two young officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, were told to define an American zone at very short notice. No experts on Korea were consulted. Rusk later said that had he known Korean history he would almost surely have chosen a different line. Soviet troops entered Pyongyang on 24 August and found a committee under the nationalist Cho Man-sik, and the Soviet administration allowed local People's Committees to function. Koreans there enjoyed more autonomy than people in Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe, though Soviet soldiers also looted and were accused of rape.

The Moscow Conference of December 1945 agreed a trusteeship of up to five years, which Koreans opposed. A US-Soviet Joint Commission met in 1946 and 1947 and failed. Crossing the parallel without a permit became illegal in May 1946, and Lyuh Woon-hyung, the last senior politician committed to left-right dialogue, was assassinated on 19 July 1947. After the matter went to the United Nations, elections were held in the south only, over the objection of the commission's chairman, K. P. S. Menon. Strikes followed, and a rising on Jeju island was put down at a cost of 25,000 to 30,000 lives.

The Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 15 August 1948, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea followed on 9 September. Each claimed the whole peninsula, and armed skirmishes along the border continued until North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950. A UN force led by the United States intervened.

The North overran 90 per cent of the south before a counter-attack drove it back, and UN troops then crossed the parallel in October despite warnings from the People's Republic of China. The war lasted until 1953, ended in stalemate and left the peninsula divided by the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Both regimes regarded the division, after more than a millennium of unity, as controversial and temporary.
divrigi: Divriği lies on a gentle slope on the south bank of the Çaltısuyu river, a tributary of the Karasu, which flows into the Euphrates. It is the district capital of Divriği District in Sivas Province and has about eleven thousand people. Large iron mines lie nearby, and the Hittites may already have mined and used the ore of the area.

In the 9th century the town was known as Abrik. It was founded around 850 by Karbeas, the leader of the Paulicians, an Armenian sect regarded by its opponents as heretical, and the Paulicians fortified it and made it the capital of their state, with the support of Arabs and the emir of Malatya. Later called Tephrike in Greek, it was recaptured by the Byzantine Empire during the reign of Emperor Basil I. It was temporarily renamed Leontokome, after Emperor Leo VI, and made into a thema.

In the early eleventh century the town was part of the territory given to the Armenian king Seneqerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan in exchange for his own lands. After the Battle of Manzikert it came under the Sultanate of Rûm, and the Mengüjeks built the Great Mosque and hospital. The traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded that the town's people included Greeks and Turkomans as well as Armenians and Kurds.

The Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği, of the 13th century, stand on UNESCO's World Heritage List for the carving and architecture of both buildings. A medieval castle, mostly of the thirteenth century, crowns a steep hill above the town. The railway arrived in 1937, and iron ore from the nearby mines is still exported by it. Most of the district's villages are inhabited by Alevis.
divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital: Divriği was founded in the 9th century under Byzantine rule. After the defeat of the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 Turkish tribes occupied it, and in the 12th century the Mengujekid dynasty controlled it and nearby Erzincan. The dynasty later divided into two branches, one ruling from Divriği and the other from Erzincan, and it was related by marriage to the Seljuks of Konya. The Mengujekid rulers were patrons of arts, science and literature, which may explain why exceptional artists were present, and itinerant artisans moving from patron to patron probably gave rise to the eclectic architecture.

The complex stands in the upper town, below the citadel. The mosque adjoins the hospital, with which it shares its southern qibla wall, and a mausoleum is attached to the hospital. The north portal of the mosque gives the date 626 AH (1228–1229) and names its patron as Ahmadshāh ibn Sulaymān, a ruler of the Divriği branch. The inscription on the hospital portal calls it a dār al-shifā' (house of healing) and ascribes its foundation to Tūrān Malik. The chief architect, Khurramshāh ibn Mughīth al-Khilātī, came from Ahlat.

The mosque's north portal is marked by the density of its high-relief carving. Inside, stone piers support stone vaults, and the central bay was probably open to the sky. A wooden minbar of 1243 signed by Ibrahīm ibn Ahmad al-Tiflīsī survives. The hospital portal, on the west, is less dense and in places seems unfinished; rooms and iwans surround a covered courtyard with a pool, and one room served as a dynastic tomb chamber.

Inscriptions record several major restorations between the 15th and 19th centuries, and more followed in the 20th. The carving and eclectic architecture place the complex among the most important works of architecture in Anatolia, and it was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1985.
diyala-river: The Diyala is a tributary of the Tigris, 445 kilometres long. It rises near Hamadan in the Zagros Mountains of Iran and descends through the mountains, forming the border between Iran and Iraq for some 32 kilometres. It flows southwest of the Hamrin Mountains and enters the Tigris below Baghdad. The upper reaches cannot be navigated because of narrow defiles, but the valley is an important trade route between Iran and Iraq. In the early Islamic period its lower course formed part of the Nahrawan Canal, and Diyala Governorate in Iraq is named after it. In Kurdish the river is called Sirwan, said to mean roaring sea or shouting river.

The valley flourished from the Jemdet Nasr and Early Dynastic periods to the Akkadian period. At Eshnunna (Tell Asmar) twelve statues of the Early Dynastic period were found in the Tell Asmar Hoard. A brightly coloured pottery known as Scarlet Ware, painted with haematite and with pictorial scenes, developed around 2800 BCE along the river. It was traded to Susa and was also popular in Luristan, because the valley carried one of the main routes between southern Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Eshnunna became especially prominent in the Larsa period.

In 693 BCE the Assyrians and the Elamites fought the Battle of Diyala River. Herodotus calls the river the Gyndes and says that Cyrus the Great dispersed it into 360 channels as a punishment after a sacred white horse perished in it. In March 1917 the British Empire defeated the Ottoman Empire at the confluence with the Tigris, which led to the fall of Baghdad.

The University of Chicago Oriental Institute excavated the lower Diyala basin from 1930 to 1937 and the University of Pennsylvania in 1938 and 1939, at Tell Agrab, Tell Asmar, Ishchali (ancient Neribtum) and Khafaje (ancient Tutub). Henri Frankfort and others led the work, which covered the period from the late Uruk to the end of the Old Babylonian period. Of some 12,000 objects, most stayed unpublished, and the Diyala Database Project, begun in 1992, has been publishing them. The Hamrin Dam Salvage Project excavated further sites from 1977 to 1981. Dams now control the river, among them Darbandikhan and Hemrin in Iraq.
diyarbakir: Diyarbakır stands on a high plateau on the banks of the Tigris, where the historic fortress rises, and is the administrative centre of Diyarbakır Province in southeastern Turkey. It is considered one of the oldest continually inhabited cities in the world, with settlement since c. 8,000 BCE. In antiquity it was Amida. After the Muslim conquests of the 7th century it became Diyar Bakr, the abode of the tribe of Bakr, a portion of which had been ordered to settle in the lands near the city. In Turkish it was also called Kara Âmid, Black Amid, after its black basalt walls.

The first major civilisation in the region was the Hurrian kingdom of the Mitanni. Nearly every polity that controlled Upper Mesopotamia later ruled the city, among them the Arameans, Assyrians, Achaemenid Persians, Seleucids and Parthians. The Roman Republic gained control in 66 BCE, and in 359 Shapur II of Persia captured Amida after a siege of 73 days. Syriac Christianity took hold between the 1st and 4th centuries, and the Byzantine emperor Theodosius II made Amida capital of Mesopotamia Prima. The walls were built in antiquity and restored and extended by the emperor Constantius II in 349.

Amida fell in 639 to the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate, and the Great Mosque was built afterwards in the city's centre. The city belonged to the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, and forces loyal to the caliph al-Mu'tadid recovered it in 899. It then fell under the Hamdanid dynasty, the Buyid dynasty and the Marwanids. The Ottomans conquered it in 1514 under Sultan Selim I, and the Safavid governor was evicted and killed in the Battle of Chaldiran that followed. The Armenian Catholic diocese had some 5,000 members in 1903 but lost most of its population in the Armenian genocide of 1915, when its last bishop was killed with some 600 of his flock.

Diyarbakır is the largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey. Its walls form a circle of about 5.5 kilometres around the old city, with four gates and 82 watch-towers. The Diyarbakır Fortress and Hevsel Gardens Cultural Landscape was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015. The Great Mosque, built by the Seljuk sultan Malik Shah in the 11th century, is one of the oldest in Turkey and is built in alternating bands of black basalt and white limestone.
djemal-pasha: Ahmed Djemal was born on 6 May 1872 in Mytilene on Lesbos, the son of Mehmed Nesib Bey, a military pharmacist. He graduated from the Kuleli Military High School in 1890 and from the staff college in Istanbul in 1893. Posted to the II Army Corps in 1896 and later to the Salonica frontier, he came to sympathise with the Committee of Union and Progress, a secret reformist party, and joined it in 1898. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 he sat on its central committee. He governed the Adana Vilayet from 1909 to 1911, where he helped Armenian victims of the Adana massacres and was praised by Christian missionaries as a competent administrator, and he served in the Balkan Wars.

Djemal became Minister of the Ottoman Navy in February 1914 and, with Talaat and Enver, one of the Three Pashas who effectively ruled the empire during the First World War. He had first favoured an alliance with France. In October 1914 he authorised the Black Sea strike that brought Russia, Britain and France into war against the empire. In 1915 he was given full military and civil powers in Syria. His two attacks on the Suez Canal failed, and wartime hardship and natural disasters turned the population against Ottoman rule.

Between 1915 and 1916 he had 34 Syrian and Lebanese politicians and nationalists executed, among them the men hanged in Damascus and Beirut on 6 May 1916. Arabs called him as-Saffah, the Butcher. Some people in Aleppo praised him for a water pipeline that saved the city from drought in 1917. Historians contest his role in the Armenian genocide: he favoured forced assimilation and conversion, and his policies allowed some Armenians to survive. Wolfgang Gust says he preserved perhaps 150,000 lives while helping to kill another 150,000.

After the empire's defeat in October 1918 Djemal fled with other leaders of the Committee to Germany and Switzerland, and a military court sentenced him to death in absentia. In 1920 he went to Central Asia as a military adviser to the Afghan army. He was assassinated in Tiflis on 21 July 1922 by members of the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, as part of Operation Nemesis, a plan to kill the surviving chief perpetrators of the Armenian genocide. He was buried at Erzurum. In Syria and Lebanon 6 May is Martyrs' Day, a national holiday marking the executions of 1916, and the squares where they took place were renamed Martyrs' Square.
djenne: Djenné sits on the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta, in central Mali. The annual flood begins in July and reaches its maximum in October, and the town then becomes an island reached by causeways. Some 2.5 kilometres to the south-east lies the archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, one of the earliest and most important urban sites in West Africa, first settled around 200 BCE according to excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh. The present town was first settled after 1000 CE.

Djenné-Djeno developed into a large walled urban complex between 300 and 850 CE. After 1100 its population declined, and by 1400 it was abandoned, for reasons that are unknown. Djenné itself survived as a centre of regional trade. Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves passing through Timbuktu went through it, and both towns were centres of Islamic scholarship. Seventeenth-century chronicles give conflicting accounts of its relation to the Mali Empire. Sonni Ali conquered it in 1471 after a siege of about six months, and under the Songhai it had about 40,000 people.

A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai at Tondibi in 1591, and the Mali Empire's attempt to fill the void was beaten outside Djenné's walls in 1599. The town formed part of the Segou kingdom from 1670 to 1818 and the Massina Empire from 1818 to 1861. René Caillié, in 1828, was the first European to visit it. French forces occupied it in April 1893 and made Mopti the regional capital, so that Djenné's importance declined.

Djenné is a town and urban commune of the Mopti Region. It is noted for its Sudanese-style architecture, in which nearly all buildings, among them the Great Mosque, are of sun-baked earthen bricks coated with plaster, and the adobe needs replastering at least every other year. The town is a centre of Islamic scholarship, with Quranic schools that draw students from outside the region. In 1988 UNESCO named the Old Towns of Djenné, comprising four archaeological sites, a World Heritage Site.
djerba: Djerba covers 514 square kilometres in the Gulf of Gabès and is administratively part of the Medenine Governorate. In the time of the ancient Greeks it was known as Lytos or Meninx, and it is speculated to have been the island of the lotus-eaters where Odysseus was stranded. The city of Girba, which gave the island its name, was a suffragan bishopric of the Roman province of Tripolitania.

Archaeological and genetic evidence show that the ancestors of the Berbers have lived in the region for more than 20,000 years. The island was settled by the Phoenicians, who came from Tyre and Sidon, in the 12th century BCE according to the account followed here. They spread the pottery industry and the making of purple dye, and are thought to have introduced olive trees. Prosperity continued under the Romans, and the Vandals under King Gaiseric conquered the island after reaching the Maghreb in 429 CE.

Djerba was taken by Arab forces in 665, during the invasion of Tunisia in which the Ibadi sect prevailed. It was sometimes subordinate to the Aghlabids and sometimes to the Rustamids but always semi-independent, until the Fatimid Caliphate controlled the area from 909 to 972. Normans held it from 1135 to 1159, when the Almohad Caliphate drove out their garrison. The Ottomans entered part of Ifriqiya in 1574, and the island suffered under French colonial rule from 1881 until independence in 1956.

Djerba is the largest island of North Africa. According to oral history its Jewish minority has lived there continuously for more than 2,500 years, since the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem, and the first physical evidence known to historians, from the 11th century, comes from the Cairo Geniza. The El Ghriba synagogue has been in use for over 2,000 years. The wetland of Djerba Bin El Ouedian, a habitat for migratory birds, was listed as a Ramsar site in 2007, and in 2023 the island was designated a World Heritage Site.
djinguereber-mosque: The name comes from the Koyra Chiini jiŋgar-ey beer, grand mosque. It is one of three mosques of Timbuktu associated with the community of scholars and students known today as the University of Timbuktu. According to Ibn Khaldun, one of the main sources on 14th-century Mali, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili was said to have received 12,000 mithkals of gold dust for the work. More recent studies doubt his part. The historian J. O. Hunwick has shown that the Arabic sources firmly attest al-Sahili only as the designer of a royal audience chamber at the city of Mali, and scholars trace the mosque's style mainly to the mosques of the Sahara and to traditional African building.

Apart from its minaret and a small part of the northern facade, both of limestone, the building is made entirely of earth with fibre, straw and wood. It has three inner courts, two minarets and twenty-five rows of pillars running east to west, with prayer space for 2,000 people.

Under Askia Dawud of the Songhai Empire, the Qadi of Timbuktu, Aqib ibn Mahmud, began a renovation in 1570. The work caused a quarrel between the ruler and the qadi, who resented the link between the rebuilt mosque and a secular power.

The mosque was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1988 and placed on the list of sites in danger in 1990 because of sand carried by spreading desert. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture financed a restoration from 2006, whose first phase brought drainage, new rendering and the replacement of about half the roof beams; the wood now has to come from Ghana, as the local trees once used have gone. Heavy rains in 1999, 2001 and 2003 brought down many earthen buildings in the town. On 26 February 2010, during Mawlid, a stampede at the mosque killed around 26 people. On 1 July 2012 militants of Ansar Dine destroyed two earthen tombs at the mosque, and it was listed as in danger again.
djoser: Djoser, also read Zoser, was a pharaoh of the Third Dynasty and is often counted as the founder of the Old Kingdom. In contemporary inscriptions he is known by his Horus name Netjerikhet, meaning divine of body. He was the son of King Khasekhemwy and Queen Nimaathap, though whether he directly succeeded Khasekhemwy has been uncertain. The Egyptologist Toby Wilkinson argues from burial seals in Khasekhemwy's tomb at Abydos that Djoser was his direct successor and the founder of the dynasty.

Manetho gives him a reign of twenty-nine years and the Turin King List nineteen. Wilkinson's reconstruction of the Royal Annals gives twenty-eight complete or partial years. Djoser sent expeditions to the Sinai Peninsula, where the local inhabitants were subdued and turquoise and copper were mined. The painted limestone statue of Djoser found at Saqqara in 1924 to 1925 is the oldest known life-sized Egyptian statue.

His main monument is the step pyramid at Saqqara, the earliest colossal stone building in ancient Egypt. It began as a nearly square mastaba, and five smaller steps were piled on top. It was once 62 metres high, with a base of about 125 by 109 metres, covered in polished white limestone. Beneath it lies a maze of corridors and chambers, with a burial chamber at the bottom of a shaft 28 metres deep, sealed by a plug stone of 3.5 tons. More than 40,000 stone vessels were found in the galleries.

Imhotep, Djoser's head of the royal shipyard and overseer of all stone works, directed the construction. Manetho credits Tosorthros with discovering how to build with hewn stone, which modern scholars think he meant to ascribe to Imhotep, later deified by Greeks and Romans as Aesculapius.

The date of his death is uncertain, and his relationship to his successor Sekhemkhet is not known. The Famine Stela, probably made in the Ptolemaic period but claiming to date from his reign, tells how Djoser rebuilt the temple of Khnum at Elephantine and so ended a seven-year famine. Some regard it as a legend. A papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis preserves a long demotic story about Djoser and Imhotep. The Egyptian historian al-Nuwayri, who lived from 1279 to 1333, described him as a wise ruler and said the Copts held a feast in his honour called the vine festival.
dmitri-shostakovich: Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich was born on 25 September 1906 (12 September in the old style) in Saint Petersburg, the second of three children of Dmitri Boleslavovich Shostakovich and Sofiya Vasilievna Kokoulina. His paternal grandfather, Bolesław Szostakowicz, was of Polish and Lithuanian descent and had taken part in the January Uprising of 1863-1864; he was exiled to Narym in 1866 and later became a banker in Irkutsk. Shostakovich pursued a dual career as pianist and composer, and in 1927 he was among the Soviet contestants in the first International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw. He became internationally known after the premiere of his First Symphony in 1926.

His relationship with the Soviet government was complex. His opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, first performed in 1934, was at first a success. On 26 January 1936 Joseph Stalin attended a performance with Vyacheslav Molotov, Andrei Zhdanov and Anastas Mikoyan and left without speaking to anyone; the work was later condemned, which put the composer's career at risk. After the German invasion of 1941 he stayed at first in Leningrad, was refused for military service because of poor eyesight, and served as a volunteer in the Conservatory's firefighter brigade.

In 1948 he and other composers, including Sergei Prokofiev and Aram Khachaturian, were denounced for formalism under the Zhdanov decree. Most of his works were banned and his family lost privileges. The censure was rescinded in 1956. In 1960 he joined the Communist Party, which was required for the chairmanship of the RSFSR Union of Composers; his son recalled that this reduced him to tears, and he later told his wife that he had been blackmailed.

His output is dominated by fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets. His music is broadly tonal, with sharp contrasts, elements of the grotesque and ambivalent tonality, and shows the influence of Gustav Mahler. He often quoted himself, as with the theme of Katerina's aria from Lady Macbeth in his Eighth and Fourteenth String Quartets. His song cycle From Jewish Folk Poetry was not approved in 1949 and could not be performed until after Stalin's death. Whether he used music as covert dissent is disputed. Solomon Volkov's 1979 book Testimony, which claimed to be his memoirs, alleged coded anti-government messages. Shostakovich died on 9 August 1975 in Moscow and was buried in Novodevichy Cemetery.
dmitrov: Dmitrov lies 65 kilometres north of Moscow, on the Yakhroma River and the Moscow Canal, at an altitude of 179 metres. It is the administrative centre of Dmitrovsky District in Moscow Oblast and one of the oldest urban areas in the oblast. Its name means Dmitri's, and it is explained by the fact that the patron saint of Vsevolod, the son of Yury Dolgoruky born where the town was founded, was Saint Demetrius.

Yury Dolgoruky founded the town in 1154. In the 13th century the settlement marked the point where the borders of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, Tver and Pereslavl-Zalessky met. It belonged to the princes of Galich-Mersky, who lived far to the north, until 1364, when it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Dmitry Donskoy and his grandson Vasily II each granted Dmitrov as an appanage to a younger son, so that it became the capital of a tiny principality. It received town rights in 1374.

The reign of Ivan III's son Yury Ivanovich, from 1503 to 1533, began the golden age of the town. During it the black-domed Assumption Cathedral in the kremlin and a smaller monastery cathedral of Sts. Boris and Gleb were built. The town then passed to Yury's brother Andrey of Staritsa. In 1569 it was seized from Vladimir of Staritsa and added to the Oprichnina, and it declined afterward. It suffered further damage in the Time of Troubles, when the Poles ransacked it.

The Grande Armée briefly occupied Dmitrov in 1812. The anarchist prince Peter Kropotkin spent his last years there after the Russian Revolution. Soviet archaeologists excavated the local kremlin in the 1930s. In November 1941 German troops occupied the town and crossed the Moscow-Volga Canal from there.

Dmitrov had a population of 65,574 at the 2021 census. It is a railway junction, on the branch from Moscow's Savyolovsky terminal to Savyolovo and the branch to Alexandrov, and a cargo port on the Moscow Canal. The kremlin's Assumption Cathedral stands as a reminder of the town's golden age.
dmitry-donskoy: Dmitry Ivanovich was born in Moscow on 12 October 1350, the eldest son of Ivan II of Moscow and his second wife, Alexandra Velyaminova, daughter of Vasily Velyaminov, the tysyatsky (military commander) of Moscow. Ivan died on 13 November 1359, when Dmitry was nine. Real power then rested with his father's advisers, led by Velyaminov, while Metropolitan Alexius supervised the boy's education and wielded significant influence in the government.

In 1360, amid political turmoil in the Golden Horde, the khan Nawruz Beg gave the Grand Principality of Vladimir to Dmitry Konstantinovich of Suzdal. In 1362 Dmitry Ivanovich received a patent (yarlyk) from the rival khan Murad and, with the Moscow boyars and his cousin Vladimir Andreyevich of Serpukhov, drove his rival from Vladimir. In January 1366 he married the rival's youngest daughter, Eudoxia, which secured peace between the two principalities.

After taking the throne of Tver in 1366, Mikhail Aleksandrovich challenged Moscow with Lithuanian support. A Lithuanian army came to his aid, but the new stone walls of Moscow withstood the siege. Dmitry invaded Tver again in 1370, and the Lithuanian grand duke Algirdas, finding him well prepared, proposed a truce and withdrew. Mikhail received a patent from Mamai in 1371 but could not enforce it. A treaty negotiated by Alexius had Algirdas recognise the grand principality as Dmitry's patrimony. On 1 September 1375 Mikhail acknowledged Dmitry as his elder brother.

From 1374 Dmitry refused to pay tribute to Mamai. In 1378 his forces defeated a Mongol army at the Battle of Vozha River. In 1380 Mamai himself led a large force against Moscow. Sergius of Radonezh blessed Dmitry before the Battle of Kulikovo, and the battle opened with a single combat in which the Russian champion Alexander Peresvet and Temir-Murza of the Horde killed each other. Dmitry won, and from the battle took his name Donskoy, 'of the Don'. Tokhtamysh then deposed Mamai and overran Moscow in 1382; Dmitry pledged loyalty to him and was reinstated as grand prince of Vladimir.

Dmitry died in Moscow on 19 May 1389. He was the first grand prince to bequeath his titles to his son, Vasily I of Moscow, without consulting the khan. He had at least twelve children with Eudoxia. In Russian historiography he is regarded as a national hero and a central figure of medieval Russia. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him as a saint on 6 June 1988, with his feast day on 19 May.
dmitry-milyutin: Count Dmitry Alekseyevich Milyutin was born on 10 July 1816 and graduated from the Moscow University School in 1833 and the Nicholas Military Academy in 1836. Unlike his brother Nikolai Milyutin, who chose civil administration, he volunteered for the Caucasian War and, after a grave wound, returned to the academy as a professor. His study of military statistics, the first comprehensive one, won the Demidov Prize for 1847, and in 1852 and 1853 he published a five-volume history of the war of 1799 against France, in which he held up Suvorov and his Italian campaign as models.

Milyutin analysed the causes of Russia's defeat in the Crimean War and drew up radical proposals for reform, which Alexander II approved; a few years before his appointment he had taken part in the capture of Imam Shamil. As minister he introduced the levy system and created military districts across the country. Service became compulsory for all men, nobles included, at 21 for six years instead of 25. Military education was reformed and elementary schooling offered to every draftee; before his reforms the army had no permanent barracks and lived in dugouts and shacks.

During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 and 1878, when three assaults on Pleven had failed and many advised retreat, he ordered the siege continued in a more orderly way, and afterwards set up a commission on the supply failures. He was made a count and received the Order of Saint Andrew. Milyutin strongly advocated the deportation that formed the latter stage of the Circassian genocide, arguing that eliminating the Circassians was to be an end in itself.

After the Congress of Berlin he took over the direction of foreign policy from the ailing Alexander Gorchakov. The assassination of Alexander II in 1881 and the rise of Konstantin Pobedonostsev, who sought to reverse the liberal reforms, led him to resign. In 1898, on the 80th anniversary of Alexander II, he was made field marshal, the last in the history of the Russian Empire. He died in Simeiz on 7 February 1912. His reforms are regarded as a milestone in Russian history.
dmitry-of-pereslavl: Dmitry Alexandrovich was born in 1250. After the early death of his elder brother Vasily he became the chief heir of Alexander Nevsky, who left him in charge of Novgorod as early as 1259. When Alexander died in 1264, the Novgorodians expelled Dmitry to his native Pereslavl-Zalessky, giving his youth as the reason. Four years later, at 18, he was welcomed back and, with his future son-in-law Daumantas of Pskov, led the town's militia against the Livonian Knights at the Battle of Rakvere.

Through the following decade Dmitry struggled for Novgorod with his uncles Yaroslav III and Vasily of Kostroma, and only after their deaths in 1276 did he take the thrones of Vladimir and Novgorod. Two years later he founded the fortress of Koporye, which he meant to hold himself; the Novgorodians revolted and forced him out of Koporye and Novgorod. Meanwhile his younger brother Andrey of Gorodets obtained the khan's permission to replace him, and in 1281, with the princes of Rostov and Yaroslavl, laid waste to Dmitry's lands and took Pereslavl. Dmitry fled north, probably to Scandinavia.

Returning two years later to lands ravaged by the Mongols and by Andrey, he went to the Black Sea and won the backing of Nogai Khan, then the chief enemy of the Golden Horde, who wished to increase his authority in Russia. Andrey gave up his claims and went back to Gorodets. In 1285 Andrey brought Mongol forces into Russia again, but Dmitry and his allies drove them out.

In 1293 Andrey united the Mongols and the Russian princes against him. Unwilling to renew the war between brothers, Dmitry took monastic vows and died the next year; he was buried in the Saviour Cathedral of Pereslavl-Zalessky. In 2023 a genetic study published in Acta Naturae found that he carried the same Y-chromosomal line as most living members of the Rurikid family.
dmitry-of-uglich: Dmitry Ivanovich was born on 29 October 1582, the youngest son of Ivan the Terrible by his last wife, Maria Nagaya, and their only child. Ivan died in 1584 and was succeeded by Dmitry's older brother Feodor I, who was sickly and weak, so a regency council governed the country. From 1586 it was headed by Boris Godunov, Feodor's brother-in-law.

In 1584 Godunov sent Dmitry, his mother and her brothers into internal exile in Uglich, the tsarevich's appanage. Dmitry was the tsarevich, or heir apparent, for close to seven years of Feodor's reign, though the Russian Orthodox Church could have contested his legitimacy as heir. He was Ivan's son from his last marriage, which was illegitimate under Russian Orthodox canon law, which allows a maximum of three.

Dmitry died at Uglich on 15 May 1591 in mysterious circumstances. When Feodor died childless in 1598, no other Rurikid heir was left, and Godunov claimed the throne. It was widely believed at the time that he had removed Dmitry to clear the way. Chroniclers and historians offered two scenarios. In the first, Godunov ordered the killing and the assassins made it look like an accident.

Karamzin, Soloviev and Klyuchevsky supported it, but modern scholarship tends to exonerate Boris. In the second, Dmitry stabbed himself in the throat in an epileptic seizure while playing with a knife, a version held by Pogodin, Platonov, Skrynnikov and others. A third version held that Godunov's men killed someone else and that Dmitry escaped, but most modern Russian historians consider it improbable.

News of the death caused a riot in Uglich, stirred by the claims of Maria Nagaya and her brother Mikhail that he had been murdered. The enraged citizens lynched 15 supposed assassins, among them the local government representative and one of Dmitry's playmates. An official investigation led by Vasily Shuisky concluded that the tsarevich had died of a self-inflicted wound, and Maria Nagaya was forcibly tonsured as a nun and exiled to a remote convent.

When political circumstances changed, Shuisky retracted this and said Dmitry had been murdered on Godunov's orders. His remains were moved from Uglich to Moscow on 3 June 1606 and his cult soon developed. The Russian Orthodox Church venerates him as a Saint Pious Tsarevich. A number of impostors claimed his name during the Time of Troubles. Pushkin's play Boris Godunov, made into an opera by Modest Mussorgsky, presumes the murder.
dmitry-pozharsky: Dmitry Mikhaylovich Pozharsky was born in Klin County, north of Moscow. As in many Russian noble families, he bore a baptismal name, Kuzma, used only in religious contexts, and the public name Dmitry. He descended from a branch of the Rurik dynasty that ruled Starodub-on-the-Klyazma, near Suzdal. The family estate burned down in the 15th century, and the family took the name Pozharsky from the Russian word pozhar, meaning conflagration. His mother, Maria Feodorovna Pozharskaya, came from the Beklemishev family.

His early career is not documented until the Time of Troubles, when he took part in the Zemsky Sobor that elected Boris Godunov tsar. He fought in the Polish-Muscovite War from 1605, routed the Cossacks of Ivan Bolotnikov at the Pekhorka River and commanded the defence of Zaraysk in 1610. He was wounded on 19 March 1611 while defending his house at Lubyanka Square in the Moscow uprising.

In autumn 1611 a delegation offered him command of the Second Volunteer Army at Nizhny Novgorod. He agreed on condition that Kuzma Minin, a representative of the city's merchants, assist him. The army spent half a year at Yaroslavl, and on 18 August 1612 it encamped near Moscow. Pozharsky fought the relief force of Hetman Chodkiewicz for four days, while Prince Dmitry Trubetskoy captured the provisions meant for the Poles in the Kremlin. Famine followed, and the garrison surrendered in October on a promise of safe passage. Most of the Poles were nonetheless slaughtered, Trubetskoy's Cossacks attacking and robbing the prisoners.

Pozharsky and Trubetskoy headed the government for half a year until a new tsar was elected, and Pozharsky was made a boyar. The system of mestnichestvo kept him from supreme command in later campaigns. He managed several state offices, governed Novgorod in 1628–30 and built churches, among them the Kazan Cathedral beside Red Square. He married twice and had three sons, and his line died out with his grandson in 1685. Mikhail I gave him the title Saviour of the Fatherland, and a bronze Monument to Minin and Pozharsky was erected on Red Square during the Napoleonic Wars.
dmitry-shemyaka: Dmitry was the second son of Yury of Zvenigorod and Anastasia of Smolensk and a grandson of Dmitri Donskoi; his patrimony was the rich northern town of Galich-Mersky. The war over Moscow grew from Donskoi's will, which named his son Vasily I as heir and Yury after him if Vasily left no son. When Vasily I died in 1425, Yury claimed the throne by the old custom of succession from elder to younger brother, against Vasily's son, Vasily II. Dmitry took part in all his father's campaigns, which ended with Yury taking Moscow in 1433; Yury died there in 1434.

Dmitry and his younger brother Dmitry Krasny at first allied with Vasily II against their elder brother, Vasily Kosoy, who had proclaimed himself grand prince, and were rewarded with Uglich and Rzhev. The next year Dmitry came to Moscow to invite Vasily to his wedding with a princess of Yaroslavl but was taken prisoner as a supporter of Kosoy. Released before the decisive clash, he did not help Kosoy, who was defeated on the Cheryokha River in 1436 and blinded. Sent against the exiled khan Ulugh Muhammad, he was defeated at Belyov.

In 1445 Vasily II was taken prisoner by Tatar forces outside Suzdal. After his release, Shemyaka seized Moscow, had him blinded and proclaimed himself Grand Prince of Vladimir, a claim he could make because his father had sat on the throne. Lacking support among the Moscow boyars, he withdrew to Lake Chukhloma. He went on plotting despite several peace treaties until defeats in 1450 and 1452 drove him to Novgorod.

On 17 July 1453 he was poisoned at dinner in the Gorodishche, the princely compound of Novgorod, by a cook bribed by Muscovite agents; Nikolai Karamzin wrote of the grand prince's "indecent joy" at the news. Chronicles place his burial in the Yuriev Monastery, but twentieth-century excavations suggest he lies in the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom, in a grave misidentified since at least 1616. His wife and son fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. His name survives in the expression Shemyakin sud, a hasty and unfair judgement, from a 17th-century tale, though modern researchers question whether its judge is the same man.
dnieper: The Dnieper, also called the Dnipro or Dnepr, rises in the sedge bogs of the Valdai Hills near Smolensk in central Russia, at an elevation of 220 m. It is about 2,200 km long and drains a basin of 504,000 square kilometres. Of its length, 485 km are in Russia, 700 km in Belarus and 1,095 km in Ukraine, and for 115 km it forms the border between Belarus and Ukraine. It is the longest river of Ukraine and of Belarus. The Dnieper meets the Southern Bug in the Dnieper-Bug estuary, where the city of Kherson stands. Almost 2,000 km are navigable, as far as Dorogobuzh.

Herodotus called the river Borysthenes, a name derived from a Scythian form meaning either yellow place or place of beavers, and a later name was Danapris. In antiquity it was part of the Amber Road trade routes. The modern names all come from Old East Slavic Dŭněprŭ, whose origin is disputed. One derivation is from a Sarmatian or Scythian name meaning farther river or deep river, the latter because the river has few fords.

The Dnieper Rapids lay on the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks, which the Kyiv Chronicle mentions. The route was probably established in the late 8th and early 9th centuries and gained importance from the 10th until the early 11th century. The middle course had nine major rapids and 30 to 40 smaller ones, and the Varangians had to portage their ships round seven of them while guarding against Pecheneg nomads. During the Ruin of the later 17th century the area was contested between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Russian Empire, and the river came to divide what is now Ukraine into right-bank and left-bank areas.

In the Soviet period the river was harnessed for hydroelectric power. The first plant, the Dnieper Hydroelectric Station near Zaporizhzhia, was built between 1927 and 1932, and it flooded the rapids. It was destroyed in World War II and rebuilt between 1944 and 1950. Its output was 558 MW at first and 750 MW after the rebuilding, supplying 3.5 billion kWh of electricity a year.

Six sets of dams and hydroelectric stations stand between the mouth of the Pripyat and Kakhovka, and the reservoirs have large ship locks that allow vessels access as far as the port of Kyiv. The Dnieper-Bug Canal links the river to other waterways in Europe. The Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant lies beside the mouth of the Pripyat, a tributary of the Dnieper. The Dnieper is one of the national symbols of Ukraine and is named in its national anthem.
dniester: The Dniester rises in Ukraine near the city of Turka, close to the border with Poland, and flows toward the Black Sea. Part of its course marks the border of Ukraine and Moldova. It then runs through Moldova for 398 kilometres, and later forms a further stretch of the Moldova-Ukraine border before it crosses Ukraine to the sea, where its estuary forms the Dniester Liman. Along the lower half of the river the western bank is high and hilly and the eastern one low and flat. The river is regarded as the de facto end of the Eurasian Steppe.

In the Neolithic the river lay at the centre of the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture, which flourished in this area from roughly 5300 to 2600 BCE and left thousands of archaeological sites. Its settlements held up to 15,000 inhabitants, among the first large farming communities in the world. The Greeks called the river Tyras, from a Scythian word meaning rapid. Herodotus said that it rose in a large lake, Ptolemy placed its sources in the Carpathian Mountains, and Strabo wrote that they were unknown. It formed part of the boundary between Dacia and Sarmatia.

The river formed the northeastern border of the Bulgarian Empire in the 7th to 10th centuries. According to Constantine VII, the Varangians used boats on the Dniester and Dnieper on their trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks. From the 14th century to 1812 part of the river was the eastern boundary of the Principality of Moldavia. Between the World Wars it formed part of the boundary between Romania and the Soviet Union. After Moldova declared its independence in 1991, the area east of the river that had been part of the Moldavian SSR declared itself the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic, or Transnistria, with its capital at Tiraspol.

The river is known in Ukrainian as Dnister, in Romanian as Nistru and in Russian as Dnestr. Its most important tributaries are the Răut and the Bîc. Moldova marks Dniester Day on the last Sunday of May.
do-aklin: Do-Aklin is also called Gangnihessou, Ganye Hessou or Dogbari. Very little is known about him, and most of it belongs to folklore. According to oral tradition, the Aja were led to Allada by King Agassu from the city of Tado. Agassu was the son of a Tado princess and a leopard, or in some versions a brave Yoruba hunter. When he tried to take over Tado he was defeated, and he moved with his followers to found Allada.

Around 1600, three brothers in the lineage of Agassu, or two in some versions, fought over the succession to the throne. It was decided that each would settle a new territory. The agreement was reached at Houégbo: Teagbanlin would found a state at what is now Porto-Novo, another son would take control in Allada, and Do-Aklin would settle on the Abomey plateau to the north.

Do-Aklin is said to have brought significant gifts for the local population and so to have been allowed to live among them. The mixing of the local people with the Aja from Allada is said to have created the Fon. His symbol was a bird, a drum and a club, and his motto was that he was the biggest bird and the sonorous drum, whom nobody can prevent. Many versions consider him the first king of Dahomey, although the kingdom was founded after his death. His son, or in some versions his grandson, Dakodonu built the palace and founded the kingdom around 1640 by defeating a local chieftain.

The anthropologist J. Cameron Monroe holds that the lineage connection to the royal house of Allada is probably a later creation, used by Dahomey to legitimise its conquest of Allada, since in the legend its kings were also rightful successors to the Allada throne. He reads the supposed brotherhood of the founders of Dahomey and Porto-Novo in the same way, as a reflection of the rivalry between the two states.
do-muoi: Đỗ Mười, also known as Đỗ Bảo, was born Nguyễn Duy Cống on 2 February 1917 in Dong Phu, Thanh Trì, Hanoi. He worked as a house painter before entering nationalist politics in his teens, and joined the Communist Party in 1930. French authorities arrested him in 1941 or 1942 and sentenced him to ten years of forced labour at Hoa Lo Prison, from which he escaped in 1945 and joined the Viet Minh. In the First Indochina War he rose to brigadier general and commanded at the Battle of Haiphong. In 1978 he took over the committee for the socialist transformation of southern Vietnam, and on 31 March 1978 he signed a decree forbidding private property.

When Premier Phạm Hùng died on 10 March 1988, the Central Committee nominated Đỗ Mười as chairman of the Council of Ministers. Some delegates nominated Võ Văn Kiệt instead, since Đỗ Mười was ideologically conservative and sceptical of Đổi Mới, the reform programme of renovation. He won the vote, but Kiệt received 36 percent, a high share for an opponent in Vietnam. As premier he supported the reforms, and in September 1990 he stressed the sharp fall in Soviet and Eastern Bloc aid and sought foreign investment and the end of state subsidies.

At the 7th Congress in 1991 he succeeded Nguyễn Văn Linh as general secretary and became the leader of the conservatives, while Kiệt led the reformers. The split led to the 1992 Constitution, which reduced the general secretary's powers but enshrined the Party as the leading force in state and society. Growth averaged 8 percent between the 7th and 8th Congresses. Relations with China were normalised in 1991.

Factional disputes between conservatives and reformers crippled the leadership between the 7th and 8th Congresses. On 26 December 1997 Đỗ Mười retired as general secretary, and Lê Khả Phiêu succeeded him. He was an adviser to the Central Committee from 1997 to 2001, and though he officially retired he continued to influence decisions. He died on 1 October 2018 at Central Military Hospital 108.
dobrica-cosic: Dobrica Ćosić was born Dobrosav Ćosić on 29 December 1921 in the village of Velika Drenova near Trstenik, Serbia. He attended a vocational agriculture school in Valjevo and joined the communist youth organisation in Negotin in 1939. In 1941 he joined the communist Partisans, and after the liberation of Belgrade in October 1944 he held communist leadership positions, including work in the Serbian republican Agitation and Propaganda commission. His first novel, Daleko je sunce (The Sun is Far Away), appeared in 1951, was a success and launched his literary career; by then he had stopped working professionally for the Communist Party.

In 1956 he was in Budapest for a meeting of literary magazine editors when the Hungarian revolt began, and he returned to Belgrade on 31 October on a plane carrying Yugoslav Red Cross aid. He wrote a detailed report that some think shaped the official Yugoslav view of the revolt. In late 1956 Tito and Edvard Kardelj chose him for the committee that drew up a new party programme, completed in 1958. In 1961 he joined Tito on a 72-day voyage on the yacht Galeb to eight non-aligned African countries.

Between 1961 and 1962 he argued with the Slovenian intellectual Dušan Pirjevec over autonomy, nationalism and centralism, favouring a stronger federal authority; Tito supported his arguments, yet measures after 1962 followed Pirjevec's position. As Yugoslavia decentralised after 1963, Ćosić became convinced that the Serbian population was imperilled. In May 1968 he condemned the nationalities policy in a speech to the Central Committee of the Serbian League of Communists, objecting especially to greater autonomy for Kosovo and Vojvodina, and thereafter acted as a dissident. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1975.

After Tito's death Ćosić helped lead a movement for equality for Serbia within the Yugoslav federation. He was a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and endorsed Slobodan Milošević's leadership in 1989. In 1992 he became the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, formed by Serbia and Montenegro, and held the office until 1993. Liberal Serbs saw him as one of the key figures behind the Greater Serbia project. He later turned against Milošević and was removed from his post for that reason, and in 2000 he publicly joined the anti-Milošević organisation Otpor!. His books have been translated into 30 languages, and he twice won the NIN award for literature. He died in Belgrade on 18 May 2014, aged 92.
dobruja: Dobruja lies between the lower Danube and the Black Sea in Southeastern Europe. It includes the Danube Delta, a marshy region in its northeastern corner, the Romanian coast and the northernmost part of the Bulgarian coast. Apart from the delta, the land is hilly, with an average altitude of about 200 to 300 metres; its highest point is the Țuțuiatu peak in the Măcin Mountains, at 467 metres. Most scholars derive the name from the Turkish form of the name of a 14th-century ruler, Dobrotitsa, in the way the Turks named other lands after early rulers.

The region has been inhabited since the Palaeolithic, and its Neolithic cultures include the Hamangia culture, named after a village on the coast. Greek colonists from Miletus founded Histria in 657 or 656 BCE, and Callatis, Tomis and other colonies followed on the coast. Rome extended its influence over the region from 28 or 29 BCE, when the Getic ruler Rholes helped the proconsul Marcus Licinius Crassus against the Bastarnae.

In the following centuries Dobruja passed between Byzantine and Bulgarian rule. Sviatoslav I of Kiev occupied it in 968, and the Byzantines under John I Tzimisces took it back in 971. The Bulgarian Empire regained it in 1187, and the Tatars first invaded in 1241. In the 14th century a local ruler, Balik, was followed by his son Dobrotitsa. Mircea the Elder of Wallachia took control in 1388 or 1389, and the Ottomans annexed the region in 1420, holding it until the late 19th century. Russia occupied it several times during the Russo-Turkish wars, and the invasion of 1829 depopulated many villages and towns.

After the war of 1878 the northern part went to Romania, in exchange for Southern Bessarabia, and the southern part to Bulgaria, reduced by the Treaty of Berlin. Romania took Southern Dobruja in 1913 after the Second Balkan War and kept it after the First World War under the Treaty of Neuilly of 1919. In September 1940 the Treaty of Craiova returned it to Bulgaria, with a population exchange in which Romanians left the south and Bulgarians the north. The Paris Peace Treaties of 1947 reaffirmed that border.

Dobruja is divided between Romania and Bulgaria and covers about 23,100 square kilometres, with some 1.2 million people, roughly three quarters of them in the Romanian part. Northern Dobruja forms the counties of Constanța and Tulcea, with the cities of Constanța, Tulcea, Medgidia and Mangalia. Southern Dobruja belongs to the provinces of Dobrich and Silistra, whose main towns bear those names. In Romania, 14 November is observed as Dobruja Day.
doctrine-of-lapse: The policy was not Dalhousie's invention. In 1824 the East India Company took over the princely state of Kittur when Queen Kittur Chennamma, after the deaths of her husband and son, adopted a new son and tried to make him heir, which the British refused to accept. After the Court of Directors set out the doctrine early in 1834, the Company annexed Mandvi in 1839, Colaba and Jalaun in 1840, and Surat in 1842, before Dalhousie became Governor-General.

Under Dalhousie the Company took Satara in 1848, Jaitpur and Sambalpur in 1849, Baghal in 1850, Udaipur in Chhattisgarh in 1852, Jhansi in 1853, Nagpur in 1854, and Tanjore and Arcot in 1855. Awadh, annexed in 1856, is widely believed to have been taken under the doctrine, but Dalhousie annexed it on the pretext of misgovernment. By these annexations the Company added about four million pounds sterling a year to its revenue. Udaipur had local princely rule restored in 1860.

By 1848 the British ruled the Madras, Bombay and Bengal Presidencies, Assam, Mysore and the Punjab directly and many princely states indirectly, and most remaining rulers were too weak to resist. Unwilling to spend large sums of money and soldiers, they had little choice but to give way.

Many Indians considered the doctrine illegitimate, and the resentment it caused was one of the causes of the uprising of 1857, when disbanded soldiers and others rallied behind the deposed dynasties. Elements of it survived independence. When Maharaja Rajendra Prakash of Sirmur died in late 1964 without a son or adopted heir, the Indian government held that the family's constitutional status had lapsed, though his senior widow adopted her daughter's son, and it did the same the following year for Akkalkot. Recognition of former ruling families ended in 1971 under the 26th Amendment, passed by the government of Indira Gandhi.
doda-district: Doda district covers 2,625 square kilometres in the Jammu division of Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, in the disputed Kashmir region. Its climate varies with altitude and is temperate to sub-tropical. The Ramban and Doda tehsils are warmer, while Bhagwah, Gundna and Warwan stay snow-bound for five or six months of the year. Monsoon rains fall from July to September. The district has 406 villages and 18 tehsils.

The district was once largely inhabited by a Sarazi population before settlers arrived from Kashmir, and Kashmiri populations settled there in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its early history is poorly documented. Various groups, including Ranas, Rajas and independent chiefs, ruled it, and in 1822 Maharaja Gulab Singh conquered Doda, which became the winter capital of the Kishtwar state. The English traveller G. T. Vigne visited in 1829 and described the rope bridges over the Chenab. In 1846 Doda and Kishtwar became part of the new state of Jammu and Kashmir after the Amritsar pact.

Bhaderwah was a principality whose recorded history goes back to the Rajatarangini of Kalhana. It passed to Chamba in 1821 and to the Jammu Darbar in 1846. In 1948 the Udhampur district was partitioned and a Doda district was formed from the Ramban, Bhadarwah, Thathri and Kishtwar tehsils. Ramban became a separate district in 2006, as did Kishtwar. In the 1990s and 2000s the district saw militant violence, including massacres of Hindu villagers in 1998, 2001 and 2006. On 13 June 2023 an earthquake of magnitude 5.0 centred near Thathri damaged buildings in Bhaderwah and Kishtwar.

The 2011 census gave the district 409,936 people. Muslims made up 53.82 percent and Hindus 45.77 percent. The Muslims are mostly ethnic Kashmiris, and a study in 2014 found about 40 percent of the population speaking Kashmiri. Pahadi languages such as Bhadarwahi and Sarazi form the second largest group, and others speak Gojri and Dogri. The town of Doda is the headquarters. The district has three assembly constituencies and is part of the Udhampur Lok Sabha constituency.
dodecanese: The Dodecanese are a group of 15 larger and about 150 smaller islands in the south-eastern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Anatolia, of which 26 are inhabited. They mark the eastern limit of the Sea of Crete and belong to the wider Southern Sporades. Rhodes has been the dominant island since antiquity, and Kos and Patmos are historically the most important of the others. The name means the Twelve Islands. In the Byzantine period it referred to twelve Cyclades islands around Delos, and it passed to the present group under Ottoman rule, when twelve islands kept privileges in taxation and self-government. The name was firmly established by 1920.

The islands were inhabited from prehistoric times and ruled by Mycenaean Greeks from about 1400 BCE until the Dorians arrived about 1100 BCE. In the 6th century BCE the Dorians founded Lindos, Kameiros and Ialyssos on Rhodes, which with Kos and the mainland cities of Knidos and Halicarnassos formed the Dorian Hexapolis. The three cities of Rhodes united in 408 BCE and built a new capital. The Colossus of Rhodes was built in 304 BCE. Persia took the islands about 499 BCE, Mausolus of Caria conquered them in 357 BCE and Alexander the Great's Macedonia followed. Cassius sacked them in 42 BCE.

The islands stayed Byzantine for nearly a thousand years, and the Knights Hospitaller strengthened Rhodes in 1309. Their fortifications repelled the Sultan of Egypt in 1444 and Mehmed II in 1480, but Suleiman took Rhodes in 1522. Under Ottoman rule the islands paid a special tax in return for autonomy and prospered. Kasos was destroyed by the Egyptians in 1824 after playing a prominent part in the Greek War of Independence.

Italy occupied the islands, except Kastellorizo, in 1912 during the Italian-Turkish war, and formally annexed them under the Treaty of Lausanne as the Possedimenti Italiani dell'Egeo. Ikaria joined Greece in 1912, and Kastellorizo came under Italian rule in 1921. Italian rule brought hospitals and aqueducts, and a form of Aegean citizenship exempted the islanders from the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. The islands joined Greece in 1947.

The islands are overwhelmingly Greek-speaking. A Turkish Muslim minority lives on Rhodes and Kos. Most have a hot-summer Mediterranean climate, and south-east Rhodes records the highest mean annual sunshine in Greece. Hundreds of Byzantine churches survive.
dodecanese-campaign: The Dodecanese had been under Italian control since the Italo-Turkish War of 1911. Rhodes, the largest island, was a military and air base, and Leros, with its deep-water port of Portolago, was developed into a fortified air base that Benito Mussolini called the Corregidor of the Mediterranean. An earlier British attempt on the islands, Operation Abstention in February 1941, failed when Italian forces recaptured Kastellorizo from the Royal Marines and No. 50 Commando.

The British Prime Minister Winston Churchill hoped that action in the Aegean would help draw Turkey into the war, which would turn the Axis flank in the Balkans and open another supply route to the USSR. Germany, which had foreseen an Italian defection, prepared Unternehmen Achse (Operation Axis) to disarm Italian troops wherever they were.

When the Armistice of Cassibile was announced on 8 September 1943, a British mission reached Rhodes, but the German commander attacked the Italian garrison, and Admiral Inigo Campioni ordered the Italians there to surrender on 11 September. A Special Boat Service detachment landed on Kos on 14 September, and six Spitfire Mk Vs of 7 Squadron SAAF flew in to its airfield at Antimachia.

On 3 October the Germans made amphibious and airborne landings on Kos, code-named Unternehmen Eisbär (Operation Polar Bear). The British surrendered the next day, and the Germans took 1,388 British and 3,145 Italian prisoners. On 4 October German troops killed the Italian commander of the island, Colonnello Felice Leggio, and nearly 100 of his officers in the Massacre of Kos. Leros, held by most of the 234th Infantry Brigade and some 8,500 Italians under Ammiraglio Luigi Mascherpa, fell next. Samos was then evacuated, and its Italian garrison surrendered on 22 November.

Historians count the campaign among the last British defeats and the last German victories of the war, and some have called it a badly planned fiasco. German air superiority decided it. About 4,800 British troops were killed or captured, six destroyers were sunk and the Royal Air Force lost 115 aircraft.

The German occupation also ended the relative safety of the Jews of the islands. In July 1944 the Gestapo rounded up 1,700 members of the ancient Jewish community of Rhodes, and only some 160 of them survived deportation. The islands stayed in German hands until the end of the war in 1945.
dodoma: Dodoma lies in the centre of Tanzania, 453 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam and 441 kilometres south of Arusha. Its name means it has sunk in the Gogo language. The city has an area of 2,669 square kilometres, of which 625 square kilometres is urbanised. It has a semi-arid climate with warm to hot temperatures all year, about 610 millimetres of rain a year and a wet season between December and April. The indigenous ethnic groups are the Gogo, Rangi and Sandawe.

Dodoma began as a small market town called Idodomya. The modern town was founded in 1907 by German colonists during the building of the central railway. Its layout followed the colonial planning of the time, with a European quarter segregated from a native village.

In 1967 the government invited the Canadian firm Project Planning Associates to draw up a master plan for Dar es Salaam, which was growing rapidly, and the plan was cancelled in 1972. After a nationwide referendum the government announced that the capital would move to a more central place. The move was meant to bring social and economic gains to the central region and to divert development from a single coastal city, which was seen as contrary to socialist unity. The rural environment of the region was seen as the heartland of ujamaa, and so as right for a ujamaa capital that could learn from neighbouring villages.

The winning plan, by Project Planning Associates, envisaged a city of 400,000 people by 2000 and 1.3 million by 2020. It was intended to be the first non-monumental capital, unlike Abuja, Yamoussoukro, Brasília or Washington, D.C., with curving forms rather than grids, buses before cars, and the garden city model. It was meant to be the chief village in a nation of villages. Dodoma became the official capital in 1996. Much of the design was never carried out, and government offices and embassies resisted moving, so many remained in Dar es Salaam, which stayed the commercial capital.

Dodoma is the capital of Tanzania and the seat of its parliament. The Central Railway Line, begun under German rule, runs through the city to Dar es Salaam, a distance of 465 kilometres. In 2022 the city had 765,179 people. The University of Dodoma and St John's University of Tanzania both opened in 2007.
dodona: Dodona lay in a remote region of Epirus away from the main Greek city-states, yet it was considered second only to Delphi in prestige. Aristotle placed Hellas around Dodona and the river Achelous and said that its inhabitants, the Selloi, had once been called Graikoi and were now Hellenes. Some scholars therefore trace the words Hellenes and Hellas to this district. The oracle was first controlled by the Thesprotians and then by the Molossians, and Strabo names Mount Tomaros as the mountain at whose foot the temple stood.

Offerings of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE show that cult activity already existed in the Late Bronze Age, and evidence for the cult of Zeus dates from about the same time. Homer, in the Iliad, has Achilles pray to Zeus of Dodona, and mentions priests called Selloi who slept on the ground with unwashed feet. Some scholars hold that the oracle was originally that of a Mother Goddess, later called Dione, who shared it with Zeus.

Priestesses appear by the time of Herodotus, who gives the story of two black doves from Egyptian Thebes, one of which settled in an oak at Dodona and spoke in a human voice. Over 4,200 oracular tablets have been found, dating from the mid-sixth to the early second century BCE, all in Greek and naming more than 1,200 people, almost all Greeks.

About 290 BCE King Pyrrhus made Dodona the religious capital of his realm, rebuilding the Temple of Zeus, adding a festival with games, music and drama in a theatre, and building a wall round the oracle and the holy tree. The Aetolians looted and burned the sanctuary in 219 BCE, and Philip V of Macedon rebuilt it. In 167 BCE the Romans under Aemilius Paulus destroyed the Molossian cities, possibly including Dodona. Emperor Julian consulted the oracle in 362 CE. Pilgrims still came until 391 or 392 CE, when Emperor Theodosius closed the pagan temples and cut down the ancient oak. A bishop of Dodona attended the First Council of Ephesus in 431.

Dodona never eclipsed Delphi but its fame spread beyond Greece. In the Argonautica of Apollonius of Rhodes the ship Argo could prophesy because it contained an oak timber from Dodona. Ancient writers disagreed about the oracle's origins: Strabo, citing Ephorus, said the Pelasgi founded it, and reported a story that it was moved from Thessaly. According to a recent interpretation, the sound of the oracle came from bronze objects hung from the oak branches and rung by the wind like a chime.
doge-of-venice: The word doge comes from the Latin dux, leader, and the office grew out of older offices in the late Roman and early Byzantine empires. In the 6th and 7th centuries the Byzantine province of Venetia shrank to coastal lagoons and was governed by a magister militum subordinate to the exarch of Ravenna, with the seat moving from Oderzo to Eraclea, then Malamocco and finally Rialto in the 9th century. The first historically attested doge was Orso Ipato; accounts of earlier doges by the chronicler John the Deacon, around the start of the 11th century, are not considered reliable by modern scholars. Early doges bore Byzantine titles, and as late as 1202 Enrico Dandolo was styled protosebastos.

The doge's powers were never precisely defined. Several doges associated a son with themselves in office, until a law forbade any doge to associate a family member or name a successor. After 1172 a committee of forty chose the doge, and the regulations of 1268, in force until 1797, sought to limit great families through a machinery in which members of the Great Council were reduced by lot and by election through successive stages until forty-one electors chose the doge, who needed at least twenty-five votes. After 1268 the doge was under strict surveillance: he had to wait for other officials before opening dispatches and could own no property abroad.

After his death a commission of inquisitori judged his acts, and his estate could be fined. The title changed with Venetian conquests. Pietro II Orseolo adopted dux Dalmatiae after taking Dalmatian territory in 1000, and by the early 12th century the title included Croatia. After the Fourth Crusade the doge was styled lord of a fourth part and a half of the Empire of Romania. In the Treaty of Zadar of 1358 Venice renounced Dalmatia, and the title was reduced to Duke of the Venices and the rest.

The doge had a ritual role. On Ascension Day he cast a ring from the state barge, the Bucentaur, into the Adriatic in the marriage of Venice with the sea, a ceremony first instituted for Orseolo's conquest of Dalmatia in 1000. From the 14th century his symbol was the horn-shaped ducal cap, the corno ducale. As the oligarchy developed, the more important functions passed to other officials and boards, and the office became mostly representative. The last doge, Ludovico Manin, abdicated in 1797 after Napoleon's conquest, and Venice never revived the title.
dogu: Dogū, literally earthen figures, are small humanoid and animal figurines made in the later part of the Jōmon period of prehistoric Japan, which is dated 14,000 to 400 BCE. They come exclusively from the Jōmon period and were no longer made in the Yayoi period that followed. The National Museum of Japanese History estimates that about 15,000 are known, while The Japan Times puts the figure at about 18,000. They were made across all of Japan except Okinawa, and most have been found in eastern Japan; one is rarely found in the west. There are various styles, depending on the area where they were unearthed and on the period. They should not be confused with the clay haniwa funerary objects of the Kofun period.

The figures are made of clay and are typically 10 to 30 cm high. Most appear to be modelled as female, with big eyes, small waists and wide hips, and many scholars take them to represent goddesses. Many have large abdomens associated with pregnancy, which suggests to some that the Jōmon people saw them as mother goddesses. The Metropolitan Museum of Art says they suggest an association with fertility and shamanistic rites. They tend to have large faces, small arms and hands and compact bodies. Some seem to wear goggles or have heart-shaped faces, and most have marks on the face, chest and shoulders that suggest tattooing and incision with bamboo.

The purpose of dogū remains unknown. Some scholars hold that they acted as effigies of people, working by a kind of sympathetic magic. Illnesses, or other misfortune, may have been thought to pass into the figure, which was then destroyed to clear them. Unbroken figures are rare, and most lack an arm, a leg or another part, and in many cases the parts were cut off.

The best known type is the shakōkidogū, or goggle-eyed dogū, so familiar that most Japanese who hear the word dogū picture it. Shakōki literally means light-blocking device, and the name comes from the resemblance of the eyes to traditional Inuit snow goggles. These figures have exaggerated buttocks, chests and thighs, and the abdomen is covered with patterns, many of which seem to have been painted with vermilion. The larger ones are hollow. Other types are the heart-shaped or crescent-eyebrow figure, the horned-owl type and the pregnant-woman type.

Goggle-eyed figures have been found at the Kamegaoka Site in Tsugaru, Aomori Prefecture, the Teshiromori Site in Morioka, Iwate Prefecture, the Ebisuda Site in Tajiri, Miyagi Prefecture, and the Izumisawa Kaizuka Site in Ishinomaki, Miyagi Prefecture. All of these sites have been designated Important Cultural Properties.
doha: Doha stands on the Persian Gulf coast in the central-east of Qatar, at an elevation of about 10 metres, north of Al Wakrah and south of Al Khor and Lusail. Its name comes from the Arabic dohat, meaning roundness, a reference to the rounded bays along the coast. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers, short mild winters and very little rain, mostly between October and March. Land reclamation off the coast has added 400 hectares of land and 30 kilometres of coastline.

Doha began in the 1820s as an offshoot of the older settlement of Al Bidda.
