The original may have been commissioned between 230 and 220 BCE by Attalus I of Pergamon to celebrate his victory over the Galatians, the Celtic people of parts of Anatolia, and its sculptor is believed to have been Epigonus, a court sculptor of the Attalid dynasty. The marble in Rome is thought to date from the 1st or 2nd century CE and, according to an analysis of the stone, is white Docimian marble from Afyon, probably from a Roman imperial quarry. Scholars still disagree about the dating of the copies and about how exact they are.

The statue was first recorded in a 1623 inventory of the Ludovisi family collections, and probably came from the site of the Gardens of Sallust, where Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi built his villa. It was restored in 1623, apparently by Ippolito Buzzi with the young Gian Lorenzo Bernini.

Napoleon's forces took it in 1797 under the Treaty of Tolentino, and it was displayed in Paris until it was repatriated in October 1815 through the intervention of Antonio Canova. It returned to the Capitoline Museum in 1816. It had been placed there in 1733. Until the 20th century it was usually called the Dying Gladiator. Ennio Quirino Visconti first identified the figure as a barbarian from his neck torc, matted hair and moustache, and in the mid-19th century it was identified as a Gaul or Galatian.

The statue suggests both the defeat of the Celts and a memorial to their bravery as worthy adversaries. Its nakedness agrees with ancient accounts of Celtic fighting; Polybius describes the Gaesatae at the Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE as fighting naked, and it may also give the figure heroic dignity. H. W. Janson reads its message as that they knew how to die, barbarians though they were.

In the 17th and 18th centuries its pathos won great admiration; it was a must-see on the Grand Tour and Byron commemorated it in Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. François Perrier engraved it in 1638, and a plaster cast was made for Philip IV of Spain in 1650. Michel Monnier carved a marble copy for Louis XIV that remains at Versailles.
dynamite: Alfred Nobel's father, Immanuel Nobel, was an industrialist, engineer and inventor who built bridges and buildings in Stockholm. His construction work led him to look for ways of blasting rock that were more effective than black powder. At 17 Alfred was sent abroad for two years and in France studied under the chemist Théophile-Jules Pelouze, who cautioned him against using nitroglycerin as a commercial explosive because it was so sensitive to shock. Nobel invented the detonator, or blasting cap, which allowed a controlled explosion to be set off from a distance, and in 1863 he made his first successful detonation of pure nitroglycerin. On 3 September 1864 his brother Emil and several others were killed in an explosion at the factory at Heleneborg.

Despite the blasting cap, nitroglycerin was too unstable for commercial use. Nobel tried to combine it with a substance that would make it safe to handle without lessening its force. Mixtures with cement, coal and sawdust failed, but diatomaceous earth, which is fossilised algae, stabilised it. He obtained patents in England on 7 May 1867 and in Sweden on 19 October 1867. Dynamite is usually sold as cardboard cylinders about 200 mm long and 32 mm across, and is rated by its weight strength, the share of nitroglycerin it contains, usually from 20 to 60 per cent. It weeps nitroglycerin over time.

Dynamite rapidly gained wide use as a safer alternative to black powder and nitroglycerin. Nobel controlled his patents tightly and shut down unlicensed makers, though a few American businessmen avoided the patent by using other absorbents such as resin. In the United States it was first made by the Giant Powder Company of San Francisco. For several decades from the 1940s the largest producer in the world was the Union of South Africa, where De Beers established a factory at Somerset West in 1902 to supply the gold mines of the Witwatersrand.

Dynamite has never been popular in warfare, because it degenerates quickly under severe conditions and can be set off by fire or a stray bullet. The German armed forces adopted TNT as a shell filling in 1902.
dzud: A zud, or dzud, is a periodic disaster in the steppe, semi-desert and desert regions of Mongolia and Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, in which large numbers of livestock die, mainly from starvation because particularly severe conditions stop them grazing. In winter it may be caused by an impenetrable ice crust and in summer by drought. Mongolian herders recognise several kinds.

A tsagaan or white zud follows heavy snowfall that covers the grass. A khar or black zud comes from a lack of snow, which leaves both animals and people without water, and mostly affects the Gobi. A tumur or iron zud occurs when a short thaw is followed by freezing, so that the snow melts and refreezes into an ice cover. A huiten or cold zud occurs when very low temperatures and strong winds last for several days. A havsarsan zud combines at least two of these.
In Kazakhstan a proverb says that the djut has seven relatives, naming seven severe conditions, among them summer drought, early winter, deep snow, winter rains, an ice crust and a blizzard.

Traditional protection includes drying and storing cut grass in summer to feed the animals, and stacking blocks of dried sheep and goat dung, called argal in Mongolia and kizyak in Central Asia, into walls that shelter the animals from wind and that can also be burnt as winter fuel. Herders move seasonally, wintering in valleys protected by mountains. Under the communist regime the state regulated herd sizes to prevent overgrazing. After the economy was deregulated in the 1990s and worldwide demand for cashmere rose, the number of goats grew greatly. Goats damage pasture by nibbling at the roots and with their hooves, which leads to desertification, and climate change has brought snowier winters and stronger droughts.

A zud can kill over a million head of livestock in a winter. A record loss of almost seven million in 1944 was later surpassed. Three zuds in a row in 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 killed a combined 11 million animals. In the winter of 2009-2010 snow covered 80 percent of Mongolia, extreme cold lasted almost 50 days in Uvs, 9,000 families lost their entire herds and 33,000 more lost half, and by May 2010 the United Nations reported that eight million animals, about 17 percent of the country's livestock, had died. The zud of 2023-2024 killed 7.1 million animals by early June.

Herders who lose all their animals often move to cities, and Ulaanbaatar is ringed by settlements of wooden houses without roads, water or sewers, where displaced herders may find no work and sink into poverty, while others take dangerous illegal mining jobs.
dzungaria: Dzungaria, also called Northern Xinjiang or Beijiang, is the northern half of Xinjiang and covers about 777,000 square kilometres. The Altai Mountains bound it on the north and the Tian Shan on the south, and it borders Kazakhstan on the west and Mongolia on the east. Before the mid-18th century the name could cover a wider area, coterminous with the Oirat-led Dzungar Khanate. Its core is the triangular Dzungarian Basin, with the Gurbantünggüt Desert at its centre. The western corner of the basin is the Dzungarian Gate, a historically important gateway between Dzungaria and the Kazakh Steppe, and the northern corner is the valley of the upper Irtysh River.

The first inhabitants were Indo-European-speaking peoples such as the Tocharians in prehistory and the Jushi Kingdom in the first millennium BCE. The Han dynasty sent an explorer west along the northernmost Silk Road trackway, and in the latter half of the sixth century the Göktürk leader Istämi received Dzungaria as an inheritance from his father. Over the centuries the region was ruled or controlled, wholly or in part, by the Xiongnu, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty, among others.

Travellers going west from China went either north of the Tian Shan through Dzungaria or south of it through the Tarim Basin. Trade usually took the south side and migrations the north, because the Tarim leads to the Ferghana Valley and Iran, while Dzungaria leads only to the open steppe.

The region takes its name from the Dzungar people, from the Mongolian zűn gar, meaning left hand, since the western Mongols, the Oirats, stood on the left when the Mongol Empire divided. Dzungar power reached its height in the second half of the 17th century, when Galdan Boshugtu Khan repeatedly intervened in the affairs of the Kazakhs, and its widest limit included Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan. The Qing Empire destroyed the khanate about 1757–1759. At the time of the Qing conquest Dzungaria was inhabited chiefly by nomadic, steppe-dwelling Tibetan-Buddhist Dzungars. After what is called the Dzungar genocide the Qing repopulated the area with Han and Hui people, and in 1884 they unified Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin into one province, Xinjiang.

The main cities are Ürümqi, Yining and Karamay. Wheat, barley, oats and sugar beets are grown, irrigated with melted snow from the mountains, and cattle, sheep and horses are raised. The region has deposits of coal, gold and iron as well as large oil fields. The name has largely disappeared from the map, but survives in the Dzungarian Alatau and in the Djungarian hamster.
dzungars: The name comes from the Mongolian züün gar, left hand: the left and right hands formed the military and administrative divisions of the Oirats, and the Dzungars were one of the major tribes of the Four Oirat confederation. The confederation emerged in the early 17th century to fight the Altan Khan of the Khalkha, Tümen Zasagt Khan and later the Manchu for control of the Mongols. It rose in the Junggar Basin between the Altai Mountains and the Ili Valley and at first joined the Oöled, Dörbet and Khoid; parts of the Khoshut and Torghut were later forced into its army. Oral history makes the Oöled and Dörbet heirs of the Naimans of Genghis Khan's time.

At its height Dzungar territory reached from the western end of the Great Wall to present-day eastern Kazakhstan and from northern Kyrgyzstan to southern Siberia. The Dzungars made gunpowder weapons of their own, built up a mixed farming and herding economy with mines and workshops, and promoted the Oirat language through laws across their realm. Inconclusive wars with the Qing began in the 1680s. After the Qianlong Emperor's victory in 1755, the Dzungar leader Amursana rejected a plan to split the khanate among four khans and rebelled.

Qianlong then ordered the Dzungars wiped out. Qing bannermen and Khalkha Mongols killed the men and enslaved women and children. The Qing scholar Wei Yuan put the population before the fall at 600,000 and wrote that 40 percent of households died of smallpox, 30 percent were killed by the army and 20 percent fled to Russia or the Kazakhs. Historian Peter Perdue calls it an ethnic genocide carried out by a deliberate policy of massacre.

The emptied land was settled by Han Chinese, Hui, Uyghurs, Xibe, Manchu bannermen and Kazakhs, and the Qing founded cities such as Ürümqi and Yining; in 1759 they declared the former Dzungar lands absorbed into China. The survivors were called Oolods or Eleuths, a Qing euphemism for the hated name Dzungar. Groups were resettled in Bayankhongor, Hulunbuir and Khovd, and in 2010 some 15,520 people in Mongolia claimed Ööled ancestry.
